content: The types of specimens included in the analysis were restricted to whole blood, plasma, or serum. Only studies that examined at least 10 independent HCV NAT-positive samples were considered eligible. Saliva specimens were also reviewed, but only one study was identified during the search. However, this study did not use NAT as the reference test and was therefore excluded from further analysis. Commercially prepared reference panel specimens were also excluded. Studies that utilized commercially available HCV Core Antigen (HCV cAg) tests were eligible for inclusion. Examples of these tests include the Murex Ag/Ab EIA and Ortho ELISA-Ag. Acute HCV infection was defined as the six-month period following the acquisition of the hepatitis C virus. During this time, HCV antibodies (HCV Ab) may be either positive or negative, and the time between initial infection and seroconversion of antibodies is referred to as the window period. HCV RNA is detectable during this phase. Chronic HCV infection was defined as an infection lasting more than six months from the time of acquisition, during which both HCV Ab and RNA are detectable. For monitoring viral clearance during treatment, rapid viral response (RVR) at four weeks, early viral response (EVR) at 12 weeks, and sustained viral response (SVR) at 24 weeks post-treatment completion were assessed. The reference standards for definitive diagnosis included tests for detecting HCV RNA using NAT techniques such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR), branched-chain DNA (bDNA), or transcription-mediated amplification (TMA). These tests were categorized as either qualitative or quantitative. The performance characteristics of NATs were noted to be highly similar above 50 IU/mL, and all NATs were considered as a single reference standard. Sensitivity was defined as the proportion of samples with true HCV infection diagnosed with a positive HCV Core Antigen test confirmed by a positive NAT result. Specificity referred to the proportion of samples with a negative HCV Core Antigen test and no evidence of active HCV infection confirmed by a negative NAT result. A comprehensive database search was conducted in EMBASE, PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane through March 2015, with no language restrictions applied. The search terms used for each database are detailed in Appendix A. Two independent reviewers assessed titles and abstracts to identify potentially eligible studies. Any citation identified by either reviewer was selected for full-text review. Full papers of potentially eligible articles were retrieved, and two reviewers independently assessed them for inclusion based on predefined criteria. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion or by consulting a third reviewer. Studies were categorized according to their relevance to each PICO question. A list of excluded studies and reasons for exclusion is provided in Appendix D. A data extraction form was developed, pilot-tested, and finalized. Two reviewers independently extracted data using the standardized form, and discrepancies were resolved through discussion or by a third reviewer. Authors of studies with incomplete data were contacted for additional information. Studies without extractable sensitivity and specificity data were excluded if no further information was obtained after three attempts to contact the authors. The methodological quality of included studies was assessed using the QUADAS-2 instrument, a validated tool for diagnostic studies. Information required to answer QUADAS-2 questions was incorporated into the data extraction sheet. Details of the QUADAS-2 items and their interpretation in the study context are provided in Appendix C. Statistical analyses were performed using STATA (version 14). Studies were grouped by the type of index test used. Indeterminate test results were excluded from sensitivity and specificity analyses, as they accounted for less than 1% of all index tests. Publication bias was not formally assessed, as funnel plot asymmetry tests are not recommended for diagnostic test accuracy studies. Conference abstracts from EASL and AASLD were reviewed for unpublished studies, but no relevant data were found between 2010 and 2013. Unpublished data were not included in this review. Meta-analyses were conducted for each index test type if at least four studies with the same index test and at least ten independent samples per study were available. Bivariate random-effects meta-analyses were performed for index tests with sufficient data to calculate sensitivity, specificity, and 95% confidence intervals. For studies contributing data to only one metric (sensitivity or specificity), univariate random-effects meta-analyses were performed. Descriptive analyses were conducted for index tests with fewer than four studies or substantial heterogeneity that precluded meta-analysis. Forest plots were visually assessed for heterogeneity, and variability in estimates and prediction region width were examined. An estimate of τ² (and its standard error) was reported as a measure of between-study variability. The initial protocol planned for sensitivity analyses excluding case-control studies, but no such studies were identified. Subgroup analyses were pre-specified by antibody status, and the effects of specimen condition (fresh vs. frozen), HBV and HIV status, and genotype were planned to be examined in a meta-regression. However, due to limited data, descriptive statistics were provided for HIV and HBV coinfection and genotype distribution. The impact of specimen condition could not be assessed, as all studies used frozen samples or did not specify conditions. Quantitative data were analyzed using a locally weighted regression smoother to assess the correlation between quantitative HCV cAg (measured in fmol/L) and HCV RNA (measured in IU/mL). Outliers were identified, and descriptive statistics were performed for these points. Only the Abbott ARCHITECT assay had sufficient quantitative data for assessment. From the literature search, 8,146 citations were identified, and 313 full-text articles were reviewed. Of these, 283 applied to PICO 5a, 11 to PICO 5b, and 44 to PICO 9. For PICO 5a, 50 studies were included, and for PICO 9, four studies were included. The PRISMA diagram in Figure 1a-d outlines the flow of studies and reasons for exclusion. Fifty studies assessing HCV Core Antigen detection (PICO 5a) utilized seven different HCV cAg assays. Two studies directly compared multiple antigen tests. Four studies were translated from Mandarin, one from German, one from French, and two from Japanese. The Abbott ARCHITECT HCV Ag assay was evaluated in 30 studies, with 20 providing sufficient data for bivariate analysis. Ten studies lacked data to calculate specificity and were included only in the univariate pooled sensitivity estimate. Most studies specified positive HCV Ab status, and four included data for HCV Ab-negative samples. Demographic data were available in 18 studies, while the rest used anonymous specimens. HBV status was known in 13 studies, with most excluding HBV coinfected patients. Only one study included children. The Bio-Rad Monolisa HCV Ag-Ab ULTRA was used in five studies, all cohort or cross-sectional in design. The EIKEN Lumispot HCV Ag was assessed in one cross-sectional study. The Murex Ag/Ab EIA was used in four studies, three of which were adult cohort studies. Only one study met the inclusion criteria for PICO 5b, and a decision analysis was performed due to limited data. For PICO 9, two studies evaluated the Abbott ARCHITECT compared to NAT at baseline, EVR, and SVR. Three cohort studies assessed HCV cAg kinetics during EVR to predict SVR but did not compare HCV cAg to NAT at SVR. All studies included patients with active HCV infection undergoing interferon-based treatment regimens. The methodological quality of included studies was assessed using QUADAS-2. In the patient selection domain, two studies were judged to have a high risk of bias due to convenience sampling, while 23 were judged to have a low risk of bias. Applicability was judged to be high risk in three studies that included only healthy blood donors, while the remaining 47 were low risk. All index tests were determined to have a low risk of bias, as predefined thresholds of positivity were used, and interpretation did not require judgment. Applicability was unclear in three studies where the index test's adherence to manufacturer recommendations could not be confirmed. All studies were judged to have a low risk of bias for the reference standard, as NAT techniques are highly sensitive and objective.
